*Figures below are drawn from `qmd_reports/report_nedlame_treatment_comparison.qmd`, which has the full methodology, caveats, and charts. This is a summary for discussion, not a standalone analysis — if the full report changes, this page needs to be regenerated to match.*

## The pilot, in brief

718 cows have received a Nedap mobility-alert (`NEDLAME`) over a ~9-week window (2026-06-02 to 2026-08-03) — the alert system's history to date, roughly double the sample size of the last review. 316 were automatically trimmed (**TX**); 402 were left to staff's judgment (**Control**). Every finding below is an early read on a still-young pilot — not a mature-study conclusion.

## Headline findings

1. **Milk production**: still no clear separation between arms. Both groups show the same modest decline after the alert (~97–98% of baseline at day 0, drifting down to ~92–94% by day 30) — auto-trimming isn't showing a milk-recovery advantage even with more data on the clock.

2. **Time to next trim/lameness event**: TX cows get a follow-up visit far sooner (76.2% within 30 days vs. 28.2% for Control) — expected, since TX auto-trims. But **about half of TX's first follow-up visits find nothing** (55.0% trim-only/no lesion, vs. **41.2%** for Control — up noticeably from 31.0% last review, worth watching). The auto-trim protocol's over-trimming rate is holding steady while Control's own trim-only rate has crept up.

3. **Independent staff detection**: staff catch lame cows on their own at a similar rate regardless of arm (Control 17.7%, TX 19.0%) — consistent with the last review; the alert + auto-trim protocol isn't replacing staff vigilance, it's running alongside it. Staff still catch `Strong Decline` alerts roughly twice as often as `Low Decline` ones (~28–30% vs. ~14%).

4. **What NEDAP is missing**: across the whole herd, **67.2% of lesion diagnoses since June 1 weren't caught by a NEDLAME alert first** (cases where the cow was too recently trimmed/diagnosed-lame or already dried off are excluded from this count entirely, since NEDAP can't structurally alert in either situation — this isn't held against it). The majority of that gap is cows who were **never alerted at all** (219 of 418 qualifying cases, 52%) — not cows who were alerted too late. Among cows who *were* eventually alerted, TX's arm closes the gap faster (20.2% missed vs. 44.4% for Control) — but the bigger opportunity looks like alert coverage/sensitivity, not the trim-vs-no-trim choice. **Staff aren't fully backstopping those misses either**: of the 281 cases NEDAP missed, only 67 (23.8%) had a farm staff check (`CHKLAME`) in the week before diagnosis — roughly three-quarters of NEDAP's misses were missed by everyone until the formal diagnosis.

   **New this round — the pipeline-loss question is now partly answered.** A raw Nedap sensor export (independent of what landed in DairyComp) lets this analysis separate a *true* sensor miss from a case where the sensor fired but the flag never reached DairyComp — the exact pattern first spotted by manually cross-checking specific cows. For the window that export actually covers (2025-08-25 to 2026-07-16), of the **214** DC-recorded misses that fall inside it, **71 (33.2%) actually had the sensor fire in time** — a pipeline/integration gap, not a detection failure — leaving **143** as true misses at the sensor level. **Roughly a third of what looks like a NEDAP miss in DairyComp is really a data-pipeline problem, not a sensor problem**, at least in the checkable window. (104 more recent lesion cases fall after the export's coverage ends and can't be checked yet — a fresher export would extend this.)

5. **Lameness history**: 41% of alerted cows (295 of 718) carry a `Chronic` history label — consistent with the last review, and still mostly an artifact of how chronicity is defined (any 2nd+ diagnosis more than a day apart) rather than evidence of active, recurring problems; don't over-read it. Still only 3 cows total with a `Repeat` history label — not enough to say anything about that group.

6. **Culling**: 20 of 402 Control cows (5.0%) and 15 of 316 TX cows (4.7%) have been culled so far — close enough, and early enough, that this shouldn't be read as a treatment effect yet.

## What this suggests for discussion

- **The single highest-leverage finding this round: fix the pipeline, not (necessarily) the algorithm.** About a third of "NEDAP misses" in the sensor-covered window turn out to be integration losses — the sensor fired, DairyComp never got the flag. That's fixable without touching detection sensitivity at all, and it's worth prioritizing over algorithm tuning until it's addressed. Getting a fresher sensor export to extend this check past 2026-07-16 (currently the export's coverage limit) is the natural next step.
- The auto-trim protocol gets cows seen faster, at the cost of trimming a lot of cows who turn out fine — worth weighing against the labor/hoof-health cost of that over-trimming rate, which hasn't improved for TX and has gotten somewhat worse for Control.
- Staff are already catching a meaningful share of lame cows on their own, alert or no alert — the pilot's main value-add may be less about replacing staff judgment and more about the cows staff *aren't* catching.
- The single biggest gap in DairyComp's own record is cows who never get alerted in the first place, not cows who get alerted too late — and now that a third of that gap looks like pipeline loss rather than true detection failure, the real "never alerted, sensor truly never fired" rate is likely smaller than 52% once the sensor-side check is extended to the full period.
- Neither NEDAP nor staff alone is catching most of what's out there yet; the two aren't yet compensating for each other's gaps.
- Everything here is based on ~9 weeks of `NEDLAME` history. Time-to-event and culling findings especially will keep firming up with more data — worth revisiting this summary again once there's a few more months on the clock, and once a fresher raw sensor export closes the current coverage gap.
